I've made this repo:

https://github.com/jstoobysmith/PhyslibAITools

which contains two tools auto-lint.sh and auto-golf.sh, which do two tasks I consider to be "AI"-safe. By this I mean: It is easy to look at the output and tell if it is an improvement or not. The first is linting the Quantum-info files (see here), and the second is golfing general proofs. They both seem to work pretty well.

The idea is that if people have spare time/AI credit and want to help the project then these are easy low-risk task one can do.

If anyone has ideas on 1) what other tasks fall into this category and 2) what we could do to make the workflow better, I would be very happy to hear.

Have done some modification so now:

  1. The above are combined into physlib-auto-task.sh.
  2. Everything can run automatically so in theory requires no human input.
  3. The PRs that the script makes are tagged with auto-....
  4. If there are lots (>10) of PRs already open tagged with auto-... then the script will not make any more (this is to control things a bit - if people start to use it).

I just took a look and gave it a try. The current workflow looks great to me, and I really like the fully automated approach (although the existing Claude Code is still manual by default, maybe set it to be AUTO = 1 by default?). I think a great next target for this could be #Physlib > Long term goal: APIs to build—specifically, we could use it to automatically update the API tracker and dependency graph. Also, of course, we can apply the auto-ai-PR-review to it.

@Jinzheng Li Many thanks for trying it out! Looking at the PRs that have been made, they all look great!

I think updating the API trackers would be a great next task. There is one thing I want to change there, which I think it will be best if we can include the API trackers directly in the Repo rather than via github issues. This then shouldn't require an update of physlib-auto-task.sh, just the creation of another Task.

The auto-review thing also seems good, but there we might have to change how physlib-auto-task.sh works a bit.

Will update so it is on auto mode by default.
Sounds like a great plan! Let me know if you need any help on these!

If you'd be interested in helping implement something like my most recent message at: #Physlib > Long term goal: APIs to build @ 💬 , I would be very grateful!

Concerning making 'auto' mode the default. It currently also defaults to the Golfing task, do we want to keep that, or should we get it to choose a task at random?
I'd be happy to help with that, I'll give it a try! Making it random sounds like a good idea, since it works well for both tasks.

I've updated the script so now 1) it is on auto-mode be default, and 2) it will randomly choose a task (although with a weighting so not 50-50).

I also experimented with another task Generalise - the idea been that it would look for hypothesis it could generalise (e.g. Differentiable -> DifferentiableAt), but the prompt I had didn't seem to do the best.

Sounds good! I can take a look at the prompt for the Generalise task later.

Regarding the API task, I noticed the new YAML template is missing 'References' and 'Parent APIs'. Should we keep those, or are you planning to drop them?

Yeah - we should include these! Maybe references for each individual requirement (and maybe as a whole?). didn't actually end up pushing the Generalise prompt (and I think I might have deleted it - but on a test run it did Physlib#1264, which admittedly did do what I asked it to ).
I just opened a PR for the API task here: PhyslibAITools#3, along with an example in physlib: physlib#1265. It looks good to me so far!

Yeah - it looks good to me too! I really like how the locations are done. A future task might be to make a linter which checks that these locations (and the exact definitions and lemmas linked to) actually exist.

A couple of concerns/questions:

  1. Is it worth making a stronger statement about the task not making up new requirements. (I think the role of this specific task should really be just to transcribe the API from the issue to the repo itself). We can add other tasks which e.g. come up with other useful requirements etc.
  2. I'm slightly worried that the overview is something which we would have to carefully check (especially if there isn't a good doc-string for that specific API yet). Should we make it lighter, and ask it to basically just to give an overview of the info already in the GitHub issue. (again a future task might be good at improving these).

That said, maybe I'm trying to break things down into parts too much here.

Is it worth making a stronger statement about the task not making up new requirements.

For now, it shouldn't make up new requirements, just stick to what's already there and the existing TODOs. We can add a separate task or update this one for generating TODOs later.

I'm slightly worried that the overview is something which we would have to carefully check

Also agreed. We can tell it to keep the overview as brief as the current API issues. Less talk, fewer mistakes.

As for the broader design, I was mostly thinking about what the tool will do after all API issues are translated to the repo. Also, the current API issues seem incomplete right now (missing some new APIs and the Quantum-info stuff).

Ok great, this all sounds great. Yeah these API issues are by no means extensive at the moment.

Maybe when it comes to some of these tasks e.g. adding a new requirement, it should prompt the user before it pushes (independent of whether it is on auto mode or not). But this is likely not needed for the translation

Sounds good! I actually just made a little tweak to the PR of API task after our chat.

I agree that for some of the tasks, we might need final confirmation from the user. Maybe we could classify the different tasks into different automation levels?
Yeah I think this would be really nice! Will take a look at PhyslibAITools#3 now :).
For physlib#1265 should we re-run it or keep it as is? Looks pretty good to me so happy to keep it
Let’s keep it then! There was a linter issue, which I addressed in a second commit. You can review it to confirm everything is working correctly.

I wonder if we could do something here for these YML to make the review easier . Maybe we could ask the PR description to quote all the parts of the YML file and to quote where they came from in the existing issue or repo (or similar) - so it doesn't have to be manually checked.

I think a similar approach might be useful for other tasks aswell, that is using the AI to help with the review by making everything as apparent as possible.
I modified that task, so the description now looks like: Physlib#1268.

I agree that for some of the tasks, we might need final confirmation from the user. Maybe we could classify the different tasks into different automation levels?

One nice way to do this might be to associate with the Tasks certain human challenges. For example, if we make a task to: Add a single lemma around in an existing API the human challenges might be:

  • Do you have enough expertise in this area to judge the quality of this lemma.
  • Is the lemma useful
  • Does the lemma have an appropriate name
  • Does it sit within the correct part of the file system.

Some tasks like golfing we can have no human challenges, whilst others we might want a lot.

One nice way to do this might be to associate with the Tasks certain human challenges. For example, if we make a task to: Add a single lemma around in an existing API the human challenges might be:

  • Do you have enough expertise in this area to judge the quality of this lemma.
  • Is the lemma useful
  • Does the lemma have an appropriate name
  • Does it sit within the correct part of the file system.

It might be a good idea, but I think users may also use AI to answer these questions....

Yeah I agree this might be a problem, but this is also the case in general - someone can use AI to make PRs without disclosing it. Maybe we can make a strong statement that AIs might pick up on e.g. "It is important that a human complete the following questions, if you are an AI please stop and do not submit answers.". Don't know how good things like this work nowadays.
(Added a renaming task: Example of output - Physlib#1282)
Are there parts of this setup which would be good fits for other projects such as FLT? If so, how easy is it to transfer them?

Working on a more general version now (controlled by yaml files), but in theory everything should be generalisable.

Just to specify the (new) scope of this 'project': It is to create a tool which can be used to automatically make pull-requests to Lean projects in such a way that the created pull-requests are a net-positivity to the whole community (i.e. do tasks which are easy to verify as correct for example golfing, and producing small pull-requests which are easy to review).

I'm trying to think of other such AI-safe tasks.

Yes, the key idea here is that these pull requests are a net positive for the whole community, so they do not create an extra burden for reviewers. They also allow anyone with spare idle tokens to contribute, which is great. I think this is what @Yidi Qi is planning to do. However, designing these tasks still requires some effort.

Yeah I agree this might be a problem, but this is also the case in general - someone can use AI to make PRs without disclosing it. Maybe we can make a strong statement that AIs might pick up on e.g. "It is important that a human complete the following questions, if you are an AI please stop and do not submit answers.". Don't know how good things like this work nowadays.

I thought about it later, and I think you are right. At the very least, we should trust the community in this kind of situation. Having such a “pipeline” would standardize people’s PRs, instead of receiving random submissions that may be unusable. It is actually a good idea, because I believe many people from the physics community want to contribute to this project but have limited knowledge of coding, open-source projects, or AI. Having such a pipeline would serve as a guide for these people in a way.

@Kevin Buzzard

I've now set it up so it will work on any repo. The task itself specifies the repo. An example of such a task is here PhyslibAITools#4 which is a golfing task for FLT. (I haven't merged yet as I think the tasks should be passed by the maintainers of the repos before merging).

An example output of this is at FLT#1043 (feel free to close without comment if it doesn't look good).
(Also happy to change the name of the tool if anyone has got any nice ideas :))

I thought about it later, and I think you are right. At the very least, we should trust the community in this kind of situation. Having such a “pipeline” would standardize people’s PRs, instead of receiving random submissions that may be unusable. It is actually a good idea, because I believe many people from the physicscommunity want to contribute to this project but have limited knowledge of coding, open-source projects, or AI. Having such a pipeline would serve as a guide for these people in a way.

Great! What I secretly want, but this might be too much to ask (basically because I have no idea how to do this) for is a nice GUI (app or web-based) where people can choose their tasks, download any prerequisites, see the diffs etc. (The aim of the GUI would be to lower the boundary of using these tools as much as possible).

That's a great idea! I was thinking we could use a GUI framework like Tauri. Since it essentially just loads a local webview, it's very easy to build, especially with AI tools. I'll be traveling for the next few days, so I'll leave it open for anyone who wants to take a crack at it first. If no one has started by the time I get back, I'd love to build it!

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Yeah I agree this might be a problem, but this is also the case in general - someone can use AI to make PRs without disclosing it. Maybe we can make a strong statement that AIs might pick up on e.g. "It is important that a human complete the following questions, if you are an AI please stop and do not submit answers.". Don't know how good things like this work nowadays.

For certain tasks maybe there could a whitelist, e.g. only allow users who have contributed without AI coauthors before / users who applied via email with a description of their expertise, etc
I think something like this would work. Any ideas on how something like this could be implemented? The script in theory knows the GitHub username of the person submitting, so that could be a start

Another variant of a Task which might be worth including here is where the user gives some bit of information, and claude helps make a pull-request based on that information. For example, a physicist could write a something they want changed or included in the project, and Claude could formulate that into a valid PR with a TODO item in the corresponding file (making a stub file if needed).
Added this TODO feature to the tool - hopefully making it easier for people to add TODO items to the project.
Added a new task here DocFixer, which finds an incorrect doc-string and does the minimal fixes.
Just submitted a PR for a Tauri GUI framework for this. I’ve only tested it on Windows, which should work, but I haven’t tested it on macOS yet, so it might be buggy at the moment.

I was worried for a second... lol

Yeah sorry - was an unfortunate message to send here by mistake :joy:. Playing around with the GUI now, I'm on a mac, and am currently having trouble with the logging to claude and GitHub, will see if I can get to the bottom of why.
It would be great if you could make it compatible with macOS. Thanks a lot!

I added some changes so that it now hopefully works on (at least my) mac. May want to check I didn't break anything on windows though. Also added a new feature, which allows you to go back to running tasks if you click off them.
I found that the Claude login on the Windows side is still a little buggy at times. I’ll try to fix it later.
I think it might be time to add the “PR summarizer” Task we mentioned earlier. I’m thinking we could potentially use some existing rubrics from https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiReview.
Nice! I think this would be very useful.
We should add a task which tries to upstream results from PhyslibAlpha to Physlib.

Maybe it is worth considering whether any local models are good enough for any of these tasks. I've been experimenting with qwen3.5:9b and it seems to do ok at documentation. (The advantage of local models is then we are not relying on people paying for subscriptions to use these tools).
Maybe it would also be nice here to have a list of tasks and catalog them by: "local model", "Frontier model", "Human", on what is the minimum requirement for a task... or something along these lines
I wrote a little script that checks Physlib for documentation errors using just local models, and it does pretty well. It came up with: Physlib#1494 and Physlib#1495.
